decisions.decision: A lot number change is treated as a correction of a wrong number for the same material, so the marking is kept and the recording is re-keyed to the corrected number rather than a new marking being derived. Rejected: recomputing a fresh marking, which would change the color on material already on the floor.

Update All Lots is an on-demand action in the lot marking tool, not an automatic repair on every edit save. Rejected: repairing inside the edit save, which would rewrite markings across history with no chance to see the change first.

The repair covers both the receiving queue and receiving history, for every part, because a corrected number is rewritten in both tables and the record of markings is not scoped to a part. Rejected: limiting the repair to parts on the enabled list, which would leave stale markings on parts marked before being removed from it.

Where the corrected number already owns a marking, that recorded marking wins and the row is changed to show it, because an existing marking is never replaced. Rejected: overwriting the recorded marking with the moved lot's.
A protected lot is skipped and reported rather than overridden, so the repair cannot become a second way to change a marking a person deliberately fixed.
A lot number corrected to blank removes the marking from the row, following the existing rule that a line with no lot number gets no marking.
A recording that no longer has a receiving row behind it is kept, because markings are kept forever and no retention or purge job may be applied to them.
Unmarked rows are out of scope. The request was to fix previously marked lots, and the separate fill-in action already covers unmarked rows.

SUPERSEDES the earlier decision that a corrected lot number keeps its existing marking. The user corrected this on 2026-10-14. A corrected number that already exists takes that lot's shape and color; a corrected number that does not exist becomes a new lot and is assigned a shape and a color chosen the same way the receiving flow chooses one.

SUPERSEDES the earlier decision that a recording with no receiving row behind it is kept. The user instructed on 2026-10-14 that lot numbers which do not exist must have their shape and color removed from the list. A lot whose number appears on no receiving row is now removed and its shape and color are freed, which also supersedes the 001 rule that markings are kept forever, for this case only. A protected lot is reported rather than removed, and a lot still referenced by any row is never removed.
The removal half of the update means the resolver probe must ignore removed lots, otherwise a freed shape and color could never be reassigned and the free would be pointless.

concerns.note: The semantics of Update All Lots were inferred without the user, who was unavailable. Four of the decisions change behavior visibly, above all whether a corrected lot number keeps its marking or gets a new one. The spec records each with the rejected alternative so they can be corrected before implementation. Implementation should not start until they are confirmed.

Re-keying a corrected lot number leaves the same shape-and-color pair held by two recordings, the old number and the new one, because orphaned recordings are kept forever. Nothing breaks today, but each episode permanently consumes a pair from the palette that the resolver skips for future lots, so a number that is corrected repeatedly slowly reduces the palette available for new lots.

Found while writing spec 002: the receiving workflow writes the text Refer to Vendor Tag into the heat field when a user leaves the lot number empty (Service_ReceivingWorkflow.cs, HeatLotEntry step), but Helper_LotNumberNormalizer.IsBlank recognises only Nothing Entered as the blank sentinel. Those two values disagree, so a load saved with no lot number is treated as a real lot keyed REFERTOVENDORTAG and every such load shares one lot and one marking. The comment above that code still says Nothing Entered, so the string was probably changed without updating the sentinel. Spec 002 deliberately does not change this, because narrowing blank would change which rows carry markings. It needs a decision from the user.

Assigning a new marking to a corrected lot number means a label printed before the correction still shows the old shape and color, so the floor and the system disagree until that label is reprinted. This is inherent to the semantics the user asked for, not a defect in the design, and reprinting is out of scope in spec 002. It should be checked with the user before implementation, because a handler reading a label is the person who would be misled.

Removing a lot frees its shape-and-color pair, so a later lot can be given a pair that a printed label, or a photograph of the material, still shows. The pool of pairs is finite so freeing them is necessary, but one pair can now mean two lots at different times. This weakens the guarantee that a marking identifies one lot forever, which was the original reason the ledger exists.

Detecting a lot whose number no longer exists needs the set of live lot numbers, and normalization lives in C#, not in SQL. The preview will therefore have to read the distinct heat and supplier pairs from both the queue and history and normalize them in the application. On a long receiving history that is the largest read in the feature, and its cost is not yet known.
